overview.description: Burro (also known as Donkey) is a card game where players try to get rid of all their cards by following suit. The Spanish version uses a 48-card Spanish-suited pack and is closely related to the Indonesian game Cangkul. Players who cannot follow suit must draw from the stock until they find a playable card.

history.origins:
Country/Region of Origin: Spain and Portugal
Time Period: Traditional game, documented in 20th century
Historical Development: The game is known as Burro (Donkey) in Spanish-speaking regions. A similar game called Cangkul is played in Indonesia, and Donkey is played in Goa.
Cultural Significance: Popular children's and family game in Spain, Portugal, and Latin America
timeline: Traditional origins: Played for generations in Iberian Peninsula

history.evolution: The game has remained relatively stable over time, with minor variations in dealing and stock handling between Spain and Portugal.
history.cultural: The name 'Burro' (Donkey) is also used for a different card-passing game similar to Pig in Spain and Portugal, which can cause confusion.

rules.objective: Be the first player to play all your cards. The last player holding cards loses the hand and receives a penalty point.
rules.gameplay: The player to dealer's right leads any card. Other players must follow suit. A player who cannot follow suit must draw cards one at a time from the stock until finding a card of the required suit, which must then be played. The highest card of the led suit wins the trick, and the winner leads to the next trick. If the stock runs out, players who cannot follow suit simply pass without playing.
keyRules: If unable to follow, draw from stock until finding playable card
Highest card of led suit wins the trick
Winner of trick leads to next trick
When stock is exhausted, players who cannot follow pass
Last player with cards loses the hand
Game ends when a player reaches agreed penalty point total

strategy.basic: Try to maintain cards in multiple suits to avoid being forced to draw. Play high cards early to win tricks and control the lead. When you have the lead, choose suits where you have strength.
strategy.intermediate: Pay attention to which suits opponents are struggling with. If you notice a player passing on a suit, they may be accumulating cards - consider leading that suit to force them to draw more.
strategy.advanced: Card counting is valuable - track which high cards have been played. If you know the King and Horse of a suit have been played, your Maid becomes the highest card. Balance winning tricks (to control the lead) against playing cards quickly.
tips: Don't hold onto high cards too long - you need to win tricks to control play
Watch opponents' drawing patterns to deduce their hand composition
If stock is low, be cautious about playing your last card of a suit
When leading with few cards left, choose suits you can follow if others lead back

list.name: Burro with 48-card Spanish pack
list.description: Plays with a 48-card Spanish-suited pack ranked King, Horse, Maid, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in each suit. Four cards are dealt to each player and the remainder form a single face-down stock as described in the Spanish rules.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Variation uses the full 48-card pack and 4-card hands from the Spanish rules; engine-level overrides for deck composition and deal pattern are not yet encoded.

list.name: Burro with 40-card Spanish pack
list.description: Uses a 40-card Spanish pack by omitting the 9s and 8s from each suit. The rest of the rules follow the standard Spanish Burro game where players try to shed all cards by following suit and drawing when unable.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Variation follows the documented option to omit 9s and 8s for a 40-card Spanish pack; engine overrides for the stripped deck are not yet modeled.

list.name: Burro Deitado (Portugal)
list.description: Portuguese children’s version using a 40-card pack where five cards are dealt to each player and the remaining cards form a normal face-down stack. Players are allowed to keep drawing from the stock even if they already hold a playable card of the led suit.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Portuguese Deitado uses different hand size and drawing freedom, but these differences have not yet been translated into structured engine overrides.

list.name: Burro em Pé (Portugal)
list.description: Portuguese variant where the undealt cards are split into two halves and stood upright in a Λ shape. Players draw from this standing stock and anyone who knocks it over must take all remaining stock cards in addition to normal Burro play.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Burro em Pé changes only the physical form and penalty of the stock pile; engine support for the Λ-shaped stack and knock-over penalty is not yet encoded in overrides.

list.name: Burro in Portugal – first out wins
list.description: In some Portuguese groups play ends immediately when a player runs out of cards and that player wins, rather than playing multiple hands and scoring penalty points for the last player holding cards.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Portuguese tables sometimes treat the first player to run out of cards as the overall winner; game-end and scoring differences are noted in text but not yet wired into structured overrides.

difficulty.easy: Plays valid cards randomly without strategic consideration. May hold high cards too long or play them too early without purpose.
difficulty.medium: Basic suit management, attempts to win tricks when beneficial. Recognizes when to lead strong suits but doesn't track opponent holdings.
difficulty.hard: Tracks played cards, deduces opponent suit shortages, optimizes trick-winning versus card-shedding decisions. Uses probabilistic reasoning about stock contents.

considerations: AI must handle drawing mechanics efficiently
Need to model opponent hand distributions based on passing behavior
Endgame strategy when stock is exhausted is critical
Balancing trick control versus card elimination

engine.handRankingSystem: No poker-style hand rankings; outcome depends on following suit, winning tricks, and being the first player to run out of cards.
engine.deckDescription: One standard 40-card deck: ten ranks (ace through seven plus face cards) in each of four suits. No jokers; used for Burro (Spanish trick-taking game) where the goal is to avoid taking the last trick or certain penalty cards.
engine.suitDescription: Four suits (typically Spanish: coins, cups, swords, batons). Trump is determined by the deal or the turned card; follow suit when able. Each suit has ten cards; standard 40-card trick order applies.
engine.rankDescription: Ten ranks per suit in the Spanish or regional order (ace, two through seven, then face cards). Trick and point values follow the 40-card pack; the burro (donkey) or last trick may carry a penalty in this game.

scoring.description: Each hand, the last player left holding cards receives a penalty point. The game is played over multiple hands until someone accumulates the agreed number of penalty points and loses.
scoring.winCondition: Avoid being the last player with cards; when a player reaches the agreed penalty point total they lose and the others are considered winners.
